passage: I'm Sabina, and Karthik lives across the corridor from us. He finished his engineering degree in May, and since then I've watched a strange thing. He keeps three tabs open on his laptop: a master's in Germany, a job in Chennai, a government exam form. Most evenings he sits on the shared landing, reads them, makes a list, sighs and shuts the laptop. "If I pick the wrong one, that's it, my whole life goes that way," he told my father once. In July the Chennai company emailed him twice. He didn't reply. In August the exam deadline passed while he was still comparing coaching centres. I don't really know what goes on inside him. He jokes a lot. But last week the Germany deadline slipped by too, and he just sat on the landing for a long time.

qa.q: What three options did Karthik keep open on the laptop?
qa.a: A master's in Germany, a job in Chennai and a government exam form.

qa.q: Why does not choosing seem safer to Karthik?
qa.a: He fears any choice is permanent, saying his whole life will go one way if he picks wrong, so waiting feels like keeping every door open.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what could Karthik have done then?
qa.a: July, when the Chennai company emailed twice; replying to ask for time, or picking one option to try first, would have kept a door open instead of letting deadlines choose.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Karthik's summer?
qa.a: Sabina watches the same evening routine and the missed deadlines, notices both the jokes and the long silence on the landing, and can only guess how he feels.

grounding: A neighbour observes a graduate who cannot choose among options until deadlines pass, so not choosing becomes the choice.

passage:
June 3: Tushar printed two job ads and a college brochure and pinned them above his desk. "I'll decide by Friday," he told Ganga on the phone. Each one had a flaw: the startup might fold, the bank job looked dull, the MBA meant a loan. He wrote pros and cons until both sides of the page were full.
June 21: Ganga asked again. "Almost," Tushar said. The truth was he had opened the bank's form four times and stopped at the submit button each time. Once it's sent, he thought, I can't take it back.
July 10: The startup had hired someone else. The MBA round had closed. Only the bank form was still open, with two days left. Tushar stared at the wall of paper. Nobody had chosen for him, and still most of it had been chosen.

qa.q: What did Tushar pin above his desk on June 3?
qa.a: Two job ads and a college brochure.

qa.q: What was Tushar worried about each time he stopped at the submit button?
qa.a: He feared a sent form could not be taken back, so pressing submit felt like locking himself into a possible mistake.

qa.q: What small step at the June 21 point could have helped Tushar?
qa.a: Sending the bank application while still thinking, since applying is not the same as accepting; that would keep options open instead of losing them.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ganga to keep hearing "Almost"?
qa.a: Ganga may feel concerned and a little helpless, wanting to support Tushar without pushing a choice on him while the chances close one by one.

grounding: Across several weeks a graduate stalls on applications because each feels irreversible, and deadlines make the choice instead.

passage: Ira, you remind me of myself at twenty-one. When I finished my B.Com in Indore, I had an offer from a bank in Mumbai, a seat for CA coaching, and my uncle's offer to join his shop. My father said, "Aadhya, choose." I couldn't. Mumbai meant leaving everyone; CA meant three more years of exams; the shop meant I'd never know what I could have done. Each one felt like a door that would lock behind me. So I waited, and told everyone I was thinking. The bank filled its post. The coaching batch started without me. Six months later I was at the shop anyway, not because I picked it, but because it was the only thing left. Now, tell me, what are you waiting on?

qa.q: What three options did Aadhya have after the B.Com?
qa.a: An offer from a bank in Mumbai, a seat for CA coaching, and the uncle's offer to join his shop.

qa.q: Why did waiting feel safer to young Aadhya?
qa.a: Every option felt like a door that would lock behind; not choosing seemed to avoid a mistake, even as the options disappeared one by one.

qa.q: What choice could young Aadhya have made to keep some control?
qa.a: Applying for more than one option, or picking one to try for a set time, so that the shop would have been a choice rather than the leftover.

qa.q: What might Ira feel when asked "what are you waiting on?"
qa.a: Ira may feel caught but not judged, since Aadhya has just confessed the same habit; the story invites Ira to name the stuck decision.

grounding: An elder recalls delaying a post-graduation choice until only one option was left, showing how not choosing becomes a choice.

passage: Bhavna had finished her B.Sc. in May and had three forms open on her laptop: a lab assistant job in Nashik, a master's in Pune, and a fellowship that would place her in a village school for two years. All three closed on Friday. On Wednesday the power went out for most of the afternoon, and her phone data was nearly gone. Her brother Kunal found her sitting in the dark with the laptop at nine percent. "Just pick one and send it." "What if it's the wrong one? The fellowship is two whole years. The master's means a loan. The job might be a dead end." The battery died. Bhavna felt, strangely, relieved. On Saturday morning she opened the portal: all three closed. She hadn't said no to anything. She just hadn't said yes.

qa.q: When did all three forms close?
qa.a: All three closed on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna feel relieved when the battery died?
qa.a: Every option felt risky and hard to undo, so the dead battery took the choice out of her hands for a while and put off the fear of choosing wrong.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what small step could have helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: Waiting let the deadline choose for her; she could have sent even one or all of the forms, since applying keeps doors open and isn't the final decision.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel on Saturday seeing all three closed?
qa.a: Kunal might feel frustrated and sad for his sister after urging her to pick one, and worried about how she is taking the lost chances 😔

grounding: A graduate delays applying because each option feels risky and permanent, and the deadlines pass, making the choice by default.

passage: In the Chennai flat, Tarun's desk had two printouts taped above it: an offer letter from a logistics firm in Coimbatore and an admission letter for an MBA in Bangalore. The firm wanted an answer within two weeks. Tarun made a spreadsheet of pros and cons, then a second one with weights. Every evening his roommate Anand asked, "Decided?" and every evening Tarun said, "Almost. I just need to be sure." What if the job was a trap? What if the loan swallowed him? On day fourteen he was still adding rows. On day fifteen the HR email arrived: the offer had gone to another candidate. Tarun stared at the screen. The MBA was the only door left, and he hadn't chosen it at all.

qa.q: What did Tarun make to compare the two options?
qa.a: Tarun made a spreadsheet of pros and cons, then a second one with weights.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep saying 'Almost. I just need to be sure'?
qa.a: Both paths looked risky and permanent to him, so staying undecided felt safer than making a wrong choice he couldn't undo.

qa.q: What turning point shows the cost of waiting, and what could Tarun have done differently?
qa.a: The HR email on day fifteen, when the job went to someone else and the choice was made for him; he could have set an earlier decision day and accepted that neither option would feel certain.

qa.q: How might Anand see those evenings of 'Decided?'
qa.a: Anand may have grown uneasy watching the spreadsheets grow while the deadline shrank, and might wish they had offered to talk it through sooner.

grounding: A graduate keeps weighing two paths because each feels risky and irreversible, until one closes and the other is left by default.

passage:
Dear Madhuri,

It's been four months since our convocation, and you asked whether I've applied anywhere. The honest answer is no, and I'm writing because I can't say it out loud.

There are three paths on my desk: the master's in Delhi, the analyst job in Bengaluru, the NGO fellowship in Odisha. Each time I open a form, I think, what if this is the wrong one and I can't undo it? So I close it and research some more. It feels careful, like I'm protecting myself.

Last week the Delhi deadline passed. I didn't choose not to go. I just didn't choose, and that turned out to be the same thing.

Could we talk on Sunday? Maybe you can help me pick one to try, not the perfect one.

Love,
Sunaina

qa.q: Which deadline passed last week?
qa.a: The Delhi deadline passed last week.

qa.q: Why does not applying feel safer to Sunaina?
qa.a: Every option feels risky and hard to undo, so closing the forms feels careful and protective, though Sunaina now feels anxious and ashamed that a deadline slipped by.

qa.q: What small step could help Sunaina move forward?
qa.a: Sunaina could choose one form to finish this week, accepting it as a reasonable try rather than a perfect choice, and talk it through with Madhuri on Sunday.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Madhuri might feel concerned and glad that Sunaina finally shared it, and keen to help without pushing too hard 🤍

grounding: It shows a graduate delaying applications because every option feels risky and permanent, until not choosing becomes a choice by default.

passage: Ganga akka, you asked me on the call why I'm still home in Madurai six months after graduating. Okay, so, here's the thing. I had two offers in my head: the civil engineering site job in Chennai and the government exam coaching my father wanted. Both felt huge. If I took the site job and hated it, I'd have lost a year of exam prep. If I did coaching and failed, I'd have lost the job. So I did neither. I told everyone I was "weighing it." Every morning I'd open the job portal, read the posting again, and close it. It felt responsible, honestly, like I was being careful. Then in March the Chennai company sent a polite email: the position had been filled. That's when it hit me. Weighing it was already a decision. It was just one I never actually made. That's where Deepak is now, akka. Starting over.

qa.q: Which company sent a polite email in March?
qa.a: The Chennai company sent it, saying the position had been filled.

qa.q: Why did 'weighing it' feel responsible to Deepak each morning?
qa.a: Both paths felt huge and hard to reverse, so waiting felt careful; the email left Deepak feeling shaken and regretful when it became clear that waiting was a choice too.

qa.q: What would you advise Deepak now?
qa.a: Pick one path to try for a set period and talk it over with someone trusted, like Ganga akka or Deepak's father, rather than waiting for certainty.

qa.q: How might Deepak's father see the months of waiting?
qa.a: Deepak's father might feel frustrated or worried, since he wanted the coaching path and saw no decision being made either way.

grounding: It shows a graduate who delayed because each option felt risky and irreversible, until waiting chose for Deepak by default.

passage:
Monday, early June. Kashish spread the three brochures across her bed in the Jaipur flat: design school in Pune, a paid internship at a textile studio, a gap year at her aunt's weaving centre. "I'll decide this week," she told her brother Deepak, who was eating toast in the doorway.

Two weeks later, a Saturday. The brochures had moved to the desk, now under a pile of clothes. Deepak asked about the internship. "Still comparing," Kashish said, scrolling reviews on her phone. She had read each review page so many times she could quote them.

Late July, a Thursday. The internship posting had vanished from the studio's website. Kashish sat on the floor, reading the design school's email: seats full for this year. Only her aunt's offer was still open, not because she had picked it, but because it was the one without a date. "I didn't choose," she said quietly. Deepak sat down beside her.

qa.q: How many brochures did Kashish spread across her bed?
qa.a: Three brochures: design school, an internship, and a gap year at her aunt's weaving centre.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she said 'I didn't choose' in late July?
qa.a: She felt stunned and regretful, realising that endless comparing, which had felt safe, had let two options close without her ever deciding.

qa.q: What could Kashish have done in June to avoid this?
qa.a: She could have set her own deadline for each option and taken one small step, like applying to the internship, while still thinking about the others.

qa.q: How does Deepak seem to experience his sister's delay?
qa.a: Deepak keeps checking in and ends up sitting beside her, which suggests he was concerned and wants to comfort her rather than blame her.

grounding: It shows a graduate whose fear of risky, irreversible choices kept her comparing until the options chose for her by default, over several weeks.

passage:
Pranav, you're asking whether to apply for the design job, the MA, or the start-up internship, and you've been “thinking” for four months. Let me, your Jeevan Tata, tell you about 1978.
I was twenty-two, just graduated from Mangalore. I had three choices: a bank job, a teaching post, and a scholarship to study geology.
Each felt like a door that would lock behind me. What if I chose wrong? So I didn't choose. I kept reading the forms and putting them in a drawer.
The bank post filled. The scholarship deadline passed. Only the teaching job was still open, so I took it.
It turned out fine, mind you. I liked teaching. But I didn't choose it. It chose me, because I waited.
Not choosing is also a choice, beta. It's just one you don't get to make.

qa.q: What three choices did young Jeevan have?
qa.a: A bank job, a teaching post and a scholarship to study geology.

qa.q: Why did young Jeevan put the forms in a drawer?
qa.a: He was afraid of choosing wrong because each option felt irreversible, so not choosing felt safer.

qa.q: At what point in the story did the decision get made for him?
qa.a: When the bank post filled and the scholarship deadline passed, leaving only the teaching job.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel hearing that “not choosing is also a choice”?
qa.a: Pranav might feel uneasy and a bit caught out, recognising his own four months of waiting.

grounding: The grandfather's memory shows a graduate delaying choices because each felt risky and irreversible, until waiting chose for him.

passage:
The fellowship portal closed at midnight. At 10 p.m., Pankaj had three tabs open: a research fellowship in Pune, an NGO post in Odisha and a corporate trainee role.
He had been “deciding” for five weeks.
His friend Ritu sat beside him on the hostel bed. “Just pick one.”
“What if Pune is too academic? What if Odisha is too far? What if the corporate one is soul-destroying?” He rubbed his face. “It feels like whatever I pick, I'm stuck forever.”
At 11:10 the Wi-Fi dropped. He stared at the spinning wheel, heart pounding.
At 11:50 it came back. The Pune form needed an essay he hadn't written. The corporate one had closed at 11:30.
Only the NGO post was still possible. He submitted at 11:58, hands shaking.
“Did you choose it?” Ritu asked.
“No,” said Pankaj quietly. “It was the only one left.”

qa.q: At what time did Pankaj submit the NGO application?
qa.a: He submitted it at 11:58.

qa.q: Why had Pankaj been “deciding” for five weeks?
qa.a: He was afraid of being stuck forever with the wrong choice, so not choosing felt safer.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Waiting let deadlines and the Wi-Fi decide; setting a personal decision date early and preparing all forms could keep choices open.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Pankaj's final submission?
qa.a: Ritu seems to understand that Pankaj didn't really choose, and the question gently points that out.

grounding: The passage shows a graduate delaying applications because every option feels irreversible, until a deadline makes the choice by default.

passage:
Seema had finished her engineering degree in May. It was now October. On her laptop was a spreadsheet: twelve job openings, four master's programmes, two gap-year volunteering posts. Columns for salary, city, “regret risk.”
She hadn't applied to any.
Her friend Rukmini visited with jalebis. “Still the spreadsheet?”
“I just want to be sure. If I take a job in Bengaluru, I can't do the master's. If I do the master's, I'll lose two years' salary. If I volunteer, I'll fall behind.”
“And if you don't choose?”
“Then I'm keeping all doors open.”
Rukmini pointed at the screen. Six of the deadlines had turned red. “They're closing, Seema. Not choosing is choosing.”
Seema stared at the red cells. For the first time, she felt the fear shift from making the wrong choice to making none at all.

qa.q: How many job openings were on Seema's spreadsheet?
qa.a: There were twelve job openings on the spreadsheet.

qa.q: Why did Seema feel that not applying kept all doors open?
qa.a: She was afraid each option was risky and irreversible, so not choosing felt safer to her.

qa.q: What could Seema do now that the deadlines are turning red?
qa.a: She could pick two or three strong options by a set date and apply, accepting that no choice is perfectly safe.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see Seema's spreadsheet?
qa.a: Rukmini sees that options are closing and that not choosing is itself a choice.

grounding: The passage shows a graduate delaying applications because every option feels risky and irreversible, with deadlines closing by default.

passage:
"Mahima, the application closes Friday." Seema put down her chai. "Did you send it?"
"Which one?"
"Any one! The master's, the bank job, the fellowship. You had three tabs open in June."
"I still have them open."
"It's September."
"I know." Mahima picked at the edge of the table. "What if I pick the master's and it's the wrong field? That's two years. What if I take the bank job and get stuck forever? What if the fellowship is a waste?"

passage:
Looking back at last year, the thing I notice is how busy I felt doing nothing. I'm Eshaan. After my BCom results, I had three paths: an MBA entrance, a job at my uncle's firm, or a year teaching with a rural fellowship.
Each one felt like a door that would lock behind me. The MBA felt too expensive to get wrong. The firm felt like forever. The fellowship felt like falling behind.
So I made lists. Then more lists. My friend Nilesh applied to two places in October and started one in January. I kept telling him I was still researching.
In March I looked up. The MBA registration had closed. The fellowship had filled. The firm had hired someone else.
I had been so scared of choosing the wrong door that I let every door close. Not deciding felt safe. It turned out to be a decision too.

qa.q: When did Nilesh apply to two places?
qa.a: Nilesh applied to two places in October.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about each of the three paths?
qa.a: Eshaan felt anxious and trapped, as if each one was a door that would lock behind, so choosing seemed dangerous.

qa.q: What could Eshaan have done differently in the autumn?
qa.a: Eshaan could have set a date to decide and applied to at least one path, remembering that most choices can be changed later.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have seen Eshaan's constant research?
qa.a: Nilesh, who applied and started somewhere, might have felt worried and puzzled watching a friend keep researching while deadlines passed.

grounding: It shows a graduate delaying applications because every option felt risky and irreversible, until not choosing became a choice by default.

passage:
Career counsellor's note, placement cell — Avni
Kamal, final-year engineering graduate. Fourth session.
He arrived with the same printed list as in July: two job offers to accept or decline, and a master's form. Both offers expire this month. He has not replied to either.
When I asked him to pick one to talk about, he said, "What if I choose the service company and it kills my career? What if I choose the start-up and it shuts down?" He rubbed his forehead and looked exhausted.
I pointed out that one offer's reply date is Thursday, and that if he does nothing, the company will choose for him.
He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "So waiting isn't neutral."
Next steps: we listed three things he cares about most. He will score each offer against them by Tuesday, and we meet Wednesday to decide.

qa.q: When is one offer's reply date?
qa.a: One offer's reply date is Thursday.

qa.q: What does Kamal's rubbing his forehead and looking exhausted suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels anxious and worn out, stuck because every option feels risky and permanent.

qa.q: How does the counsellor help Kamal move forward?
qa.a: The counsellor points out that waiting lets the company decide, then has Kamal score the offers against three things he cares about by Tuesday, with a meeting Wednesday.

qa.q: How might the start-up see Kamal's silence?
qa.a: The start-up may read his lack of reply as lost interest and move on, which is how not choosing becomes a choice by default.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, a graduate delaying his reply because every option feels risky and irreversible, until waiting becomes a choice by default.

passage:
28 March, Gudi Padwa

Everyone's out with the gudi on their balconies, new beginnings and all. Meanwhile I've had four tabs open since January: the master's in Pune, the job at the Nashik firm, the village school fellowship, and the government exam form.
I read them every night. I make pro and con lists. Every option feels like a door that locks behind me. What if I pick the master's and there are no jobs after? What if I take the job and I'm stuck forever?
Chinmay applied to two things in February and got one. Today he said, "You know the fellowship deadline was yesterday?" I did know. I just didn't click submit.
So I guess I did choose something. I chose by not choosing.
The master's closes on the 5th. I keep looking at it.

Kashish

qa.q: Which deadline passed yesterday?
qa.a: The fellowship deadline.

qa.q: Why does Kashish keep not clicking submit?
qa.a: Every option feels risky and permanent, "a door that locks behind me", so staying undecided feels safer, even though Kashish feels stuck and uneasy.

qa.q: What could Kashish do before the 5th?
qa.a: Treat the master's application as one small, reversible step, set a time to submit, and talk it through with a mentor or with Chinmay; applying is not committing forever.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Kashish's delay?
qa.a: Chinmay, who applied in February, seems worried and gently points out the missed deadline so Kashish can see the cost of waiting.

grounding: A graduate delays every application because each option feels risky and permanent, and not choosing becomes a choice by default.
